The Rout of Prabhakaran: When a Liberation Movement Lost Its Way

# The Rout of Prabhakaran: When a Liberation Movement Lost Its Way

### How entire generations in Tamil Nadu romanticised the LTTE — and why revisiting that history today feels deeply uncomfortable.

[](https://substack.com/@amaruvi)

If you grew up in Tamil Nadu during the 1980s and early 2000s, chances are you remember how enormous the LTTE once felt in public imagination.

I certainly do.

Back then, Velupillai Prabhakaran wasn’t seen merely as the head of a militant organisation in Sri Lanka. For many Tamils, he represented resistance itself — Tamil pride standing up against humiliation, violence, and state oppression.

His posters appeared in tea shops and college hostels. Speeches circulated on cassette tapes. Political meetings often carried an unmistakable emotional charge whenever Sri Lankan Tamils were discussed. In some circles, supporting the LTTE felt less like a political position and more like a moral obligation.

And to understand why, one has to acknowledge a difficult truth first: the suffering of Sri Lankan Tamils was real.

The anger that followed Black July did not emerge from nowhere. Years of discrimination, violence, broken political promises, and insecurity had created deep wounds. Many Tamils across the world watched those events with helplessness and rage. Militancy, in that atmosphere, came to be seen by many as inevitable.

But reading The Rout of Prabhakaran by M. R. Narayan Swamy years later leaves you with an unsettling question:

What happens when a movement born out of genuine grievance slowly loses the ability to tolerate criticism, compromise, or dissent?

## The Making of “Thalaivar”

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

One of the most striking things about the book is how completely the LTTE eventually became centred around one individual.

Prabhakaran was no longer simply a leader. Over time, he became “Thalaivar” — a figure elevated beyond questioning. Criticism was increasingly treated as betrayal. Rival Tamil militant groups were eliminated. Moderate Tamil voices lost relevance. Journalists and intellectuals who disagreed with the LTTE often operated under fear.

Looking back, this was perhaps the beginning of the movement’s decline.

Armed movements can survive battlefield losses. What they struggle to survive is the disappearance of internal debate. Once every disagreement becomes disloyalty, organisations become rigid and isolated.

Swamy portrays Prabhakaran not as a caricatured villain, but as an intensely disciplined and deeply uncompromising man who came to see negotiation itself as weakness. To supporters, that may once have looked like strength. But over time, it narrowed the political possibilities available to Sri Lankan Tamils themselves.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## When Violence Consumes the Cause

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Another uncomfortable reality the book confronts is the extent to which violence gradually became central to the LTTE’s identity.

Suicide bombings, assassinations, and attacks on civilians fundamentally changed how the organisation was viewed internationally. The assassination of Rajiv Gandhi in 1991 was perhaps the single biggest turning point. Whatever sympathy existed in India toward the LTTE weakened dramatically after that moment.

I still remember how emotionally polarised discussions around Rajiv Gandhi’s killing used to be. In some circles, even raising criticism of the LTTE invited suspicion. That atmosphere itself says something about how deeply mythologised the movement had become in Tamil political culture. Prabhakaran, with his intransigence, killed not only Rajiv Gandhi, but also the good will of those Indians from Tamil Nadu who had some soft corner left for him.

Then there was the expulsion and killing of Muslims from Northern Sri Lanka in 1990 — an episode that remains deeply disturbing even today. Families who had lived there for generations were reportedly asked to leave within hours. For many observers, that incident permanently damaged the LTTE’s claim that it represented a just or inclusive political vision.

Swamy repeatedly returns to a simple but important point: when every action is justified in the name of “the struggle,” moral limits slowly begin to disappear.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The Civilians Caught in the Middle

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

What stayed with me most after reading the book was not the battlefield history, but the sense of exhaustion surrounding ordinary Tamil civilians.

For decades, they lived between multiple forms of fear — Sri Lankan military operations, displacement, economic collapse, internal repression, and forced recruitment by militant groups. Human rights organisations documented the LTTE’s use of child soldiers during different phases of the war, something many supporters outside Sri Lanka often found difficult to confront honestly.

I remember hearing conversations in Tamil Nadu where the LTTE was discussed almost romantically, while the everyday realities inside war zones remained distant abstractions.

That distance mattered.

Because for many civilians in northern Sri Lanka, survival itself had become uncertain. Families lost children to shelling, disappearances, migration, recruitment, and endless instability. Even fundraising within sections of the Tamil diaspora — seen by some as sacrifice and by others as coercion — reflected how deeply militarised the conflict had become.

By the final years, it increasingly felt as though the movement no longer knew how to exist outside war.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The Peace That Never Arrived

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

One of the saddest parts of Sri Lanka’s history is how many moments of possible reconciliation collapsed.

Successive Sri Lankan governments undeniably bear responsibility for decades of mistrust and failed accommodation. But Swamy’s book also argues that Prabhakaran repeatedly struggled to accept partial political settlements or incremental compromise.

The Norwegian-mediated peace talks in the early 2000s briefly created hope. For a while, it seemed possible that negotiations might replace permanent conflict. But the LTTE, after decades of armed struggle, appeared deeply uncomfortable transitioning into conventional democratic politics. Prabhakaran was to be blamed for the collapse of the talks.

The tragedy is that by the time the war entered its final phase, international sympathy for the LTTE had sharply diminished — even as Tamil civilians faced catastrophic consequences.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Tamil Nadu’s Emotional Relationship With the LTTE

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The book also forces uncomfortable reflection closer to home.

In Tamil Nadu, the Sri Lankan Tamil issue became emotionally charged in ways that often blurred the line between empathy and romanticisation. Politicians, activists, and sections of cinema culture projected Prabhakaran as a heroic symbol of Tamil resistance. Public conversations frequently reduced an extraordinarily complex conflict into a simple narrative of heroes and villains.

What received far less attention were the LTTE’s internal purges, suppression of dissent, treatment of rival Tamil voices, or authoritarian culture.

Even today, criticism of the LTTE can sometimes provoke emotional reactions that have less to do with historical analysis and more to do with memory, identity, and accumulated anger.

But acknowledging the suffering of Sri Lankan Tamils does not require silence about the LTTE’s failures.

The two are not the same thing.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Beyond Slogans and Mythmaking

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

That is ultimately what makes The Rout of Prabhakaran worth reading.

Not because it provides neat answers, but because it forces readers — especially those shaped by the emotional politics of the 1990s — to revisit old certainties with greater honesty.

The Sri Lankan Tamil struggle deserved political imagination, democratic leadership, and durable reconciliation. Instead, it became trapped between Sinhala majoritarianism and militant absolutism. The consequences of that failure are still visible even today — in Sri Lanka, within the diaspora, and in the political memory of Tamil Nadu itself.

Some histories become difficult precisely because they once felt emotionally unquestionable.

This is one of them.

P.S.: Legendary Tamil Writer Jeyakanthan speaks of LTTE’s atrocities when the latter had killed rival militant group leader Padmanabha.
